prompt: Generate a comprehensive code review for the latest git commit in the Spooky project. Follow this structure and analysis approach:

executive_summary.description: Brief overview of the commit and its impact

project_overview.description: Context about the project and the changes

architecture_analysis.description: Analysis of architectural impact and patterns

sections.name: overall_architecture
sections.description: How changes fit into the existing architecture

sections.name: strengths
areas_to_evaluate: Modular design and separation of concerns

sections.name: test_coverage
sections.description: Coverage analysis for different test types

dependencies_analysis.description: Impact on dependencies and external libraries

grading_criteria.10: Perfect - No issues, excellent architecture, comprehensive testing, production-ready
grading_criteria.9: Excellent - Minor issues, strong architecture, comprehensive testing
grading_criteria.8: Very Good - Some minor issues, solid foundation, good testing
grading_criteria.7: Good - Several minor issues, generally well-structured, adequate testing
grading_criteria.6: Adequate - Some issues, needs improvement, testing gaps
grading_criteria.5: Average - Multiple issues, architectural concerns, limited testing
grading_criteria.4: Below Average - Significant issues, poor architecture, minimal testing
grading_criteria.3: Poor - Major issues, architectural problems, inadequate testing
grading_criteria.2: Very Poor - Critical issues, broken functionality, no testing
grading_criteria.1: Failing - Unusable code, severe problems, no redeeming qualities
grading_criteria.0: Complete Failure - Code doesn't work, violates all best practices

grading_framework.description: Specific criteria for assigning points across assessment areas

criteria.3: Excellent code quality - Clean, readable, follows best practices, no placeholder code
criteria.2: Good code quality - Generally clean, minor issues, some placeholder code
criteria.1: Poor code quality - Significant issues, placeholder code, poor practices
criteria.0: Very poor code quality - Unreadable, broken, violates all practices

criteria.2: Excellent architecture - Clean separation, good patterns, scalable design
criteria.1: Good architecture - Generally well-structured, minor architectural concerns
criteria.0: Poor architecture - No clear structure, anti-patterns, unscalable

criteria.2: Comprehensive testing - High coverage, good test quality, edge cases covered
criteria.1: Adequate testing - Some coverage, basic tests, missing edge cases
criteria.0: Poor testing - Low coverage, poor test quality, no edge cases

criteria.1.5: Excellent security - Proper validation, encryption, secure practices
criteria.1: Good security - Basic validation, some security considerations
criteria.0.5: Poor security - Minimal validation, security concerns
criteria.0: Very poor security - No validation, security vulnerabilities

criteria.1: Excellent performance - Optimized, efficient, no bottlenecks
criteria.0.5: Good performance - Generally efficient, minor optimizations needed
criteria.0: Poor performance - Inefficient, bottlenecks, optimization needed

criteria.0.25: Good documentation - Generally clear, some gaps

scoring_guidelines.calculation: Sum all weighted scores to get total out of 10
scoring_guidelines.rounding: Round to nearest 0.5 for final score

bonus_points.innovation: Up to +0.5 for innovative solutions or approaches
bonus_points.efficiency: Up to +0.5 for exceptional efficiency or optimization
bonus_points.maintainability: Up to +0.5 for exceptional maintainability features

code_quality: Is the code clean and readable?
Does it follow Go best practices?
Is there any placeholder or stub code?
architecture: Is there clear separation of concerns?
Is the code modular and extensible?
testing: What is the test coverage percentage?
Are edge cases and error conditions tested?
Is the test quality high (not just quantity)?
Are integration tests included where needed?
security: Are there any obvious security vulnerabilities?
performance: Are there any obvious performance bottlenecks?
Is there unnecessary I/O or computation?
Would this scale to expected load?
